cards.title: Independence of Fixed- and Random-Effects Identifiability
cards.claim: The identifiability of random-effects parameters (variances/covariances) is not strictly dependent on the identifiability of their corresponding fixed-effects parameters. In the cited examples, random-effect parameters were identifiable even when their corresponding fixed-effect parameters were unidentifiable. However, the source notes that in its limited examples, identifiable fixed effects always had identifiable corresponding random effects; the reverse case (identifiable fixed/unidentifiable random) was not demonstrated as a general rule.
conditions: Applies to nonlinear mixed-effects models (population PK/PD).
Demonstrated in the cited Bateman/Dost model examples under specified fixed/random-effect and covariance structures. Do not infer a symmetric implication or a universal effect of fixing F.
Source examples show random effects can be identifiable despite unidentifiable fixed effects (e.g., ωV3 identifiable while V3 unidentifiable).
required_inputs: Population Fisher Information Matrix including terms for random effects.
limitations: No standard rule exists to predict random-effect identifiability from fixed-effect identifiability; each must be assessed.
Interactions between covariances in the Ω matrix may affect identifiability, which was not fully explored in the source examples.
The opposite direction was not demonstrated in the limited examples and cannot be inferred from them; assess fixed and random-effect identifiability under the stated candidate model/design.
cards.downstream_use: When building population models, do not assume that fixing a fixed-effect parameter resolves identifiability issues for its associated random-effect parameter. Assess both separately using the FIM criterion, noting that random-effect identifiability can persist even when fixed-effect identifiability fails.

note: Method/reference scope retained; source identity is available in original evidence.
